title: Variables, Types, and Assignment
content:
What problem does this solve?
Programs need to remember values — a character's name, current health, or score — and reuse them later.

Basic syntax
  name = expression

What actually happens
The right-hand side is evaluated first. Then Python attaches that resulting value to the name on the left. A variable is a label pointing at a value, not a fixed box that permanently owns one type.

A string is text in quotes, such as "Rook". An integer is a whole number without quotes, such as 80. An expression is anything Python can evaluate, including a name, a number, or strength + 3.

When this is useful
A character sheet uses names like health and level so later code can update them without rewriting every print statement.
concepts: Assignment evaluates the right side, then binds the name on the left
Strings are quoted text; integers are whole numbers without quotes
Variable names should describe meaning (health, not x)
Reassigning a name makes it point at a new value

examples.title: Create and use variables
examples.explanation: name refers to the string Aria. health refers to the integer 100. print uses those names instead of repeating the values.

examples.title: Reassignment
examples.explanation: gold + 10 creates 60, then gold is rebound to 60. The old 50 is no longer used.

common_mistakes: Writing health == 100 when you meant to assign ( == compares two values )
Using a variable before assigning it — that raises NameError
Putting quotes around a number when you needed an integer: "80" is a string

exercises.title: Finish the assignment
exercises.prompt: Complete the code so attack equals strength plus the weapon bonus. Replace the placeholder so the expression uses both variable names.
exercises.starter_code:
strength = 12
weapon_bonus = 3
attack = None  # TODO: set this to strength + weapon_bonus
print(attack)
hints: Replace None with an expression using the two variables.
Use the + operator to add the integers those names refer to.
The left side is attack; the right side should mention strength and weapon_bonus.

tests.name: attack
tests.message: Build attack from the names strength and weapon_bonus, not a hardcoded number.

exercises.title: Collect more gold
exercises.prompt: gold already starts at 50. Reassign gold so it becomes 10 more than its current value, then print gold. Do not just write 60 — use gold on the right-hand side.
exercises.starter_code:
gold = 50
# Add 10 gold, then print gold
hints: Reassignment uses the current value of a name to compute a new one.
The pattern is: the same name on the left and the right of =.
Add 10 to gold, store the result back in gold, then print it.

tests.name: gold
tests.message: Give gold a new value that uses gold on the right-hand side.

exercises.title: Character summary variables
exercises.prompt:
Create variables:
  name  -> the string "Rook"
  health -> the integer 80
  level  -> the integer 3

Then print each on its own line in that order (name, health, level).
exercises.starter_code: # Create name, health, and level, then print them
hints: Strings need quotes; integers do not.
Assign all three names first, then call print three times using those names.
Print the variables themselves, not copies of the text you assigned.
